strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of common VFI pipelines: treating long interpolation as many independent adjacent-frame problems. The video-centric framing and chunk-level autoregressive generation are well motivated for improving temporal coherence.

The proposed skip-concatenate sampling idea is interesting and task-specific. The ablation in Table 2 supports that it reduces FVD substantially versus causal autoregressive sampling, suggesting a real effect on temporal stability.

The architecture combines several practical components, including local spatial/dense temporal attention, tiled VAE encoding, nearest-neighbor temporal conditioning with masks, and a conditional VAE decoder. These choices are plausible for scaling latent diffusion/flow models to long or high-resolution videos.

Results on the proposed SNU-FILM-entire and XTest-entire settings show improved FVD over several strong flow-based baselines, especially at high interpolation factors, which is consistent with the paper's temporal-coherence motivation.
weaknesses: The empirical case is not yet strong enough for the breadth of the claims. The main comparison omits the diffusion-based VFI methods discussed in related work, such as LDMVFI, EDEN, LBBDM, MADIFF, and VIDIM. Since the paper positions itself as a diffusion-based alternative, comparing mainly against flow-based methods leaves a major gap.

The claimed state-of-the-art performance is overextended. The benchmarks are newly constructed by the authors, and the method is not consistently best on all reported metrics; for example BiM-VFI has better LPIPS on SNU-FILM-16x and XTest-16x in Table 1. The text also refers to splits such as SNU-FILM-hard/extreme and XTest-4K that do not match the table labels, which weakens confidence in the reporting.

The new video-centric benchmarks are insufficiently specified. The paper does not clearly state the number of videos, sequence lengths, exact downsampling protocol, FVD feature setup, or whether evaluation uses all frames consistently across methods. Table 3 mentions only 16 test videos, raising concern that some conclusions may be based on a small evaluation set.

Key technical components are under-specified. The skip-concatenate procedure is described conceptually but lacks a precise algorithm: skip interval, chunk overlap, how boundary chunks are handled, how context is selected, and whether the same denoising schedule is used for skip and concatenate chunks. Sparse attention window sizes and complexity are also not quantified.

The arbitrary-resolution and 4K generalization claims are not adequately supported. The paper states that 4K inference is possible on two 80GB GPUs, but provides no 4K quantitative results, visual examples, memory/runtime tables, or comparison to alternative tiling/attention choices.

Ablations are too limited for a multi-component system. There is no ablation for local attention versus full/window variants, tiled VAE encoding, temporal chunk length, skip frequency, number of sampling steps, training data scale, or the effect of initializing from Wan2.1. The conditional VAE and skip-concatenate results are useful but do not isolate most architectural claims.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says source code is available but the link is blank. Important details such as model size, attention window parameters, exact benchmark construction scripts, hardware/training time, inference latency, and baseline settings are missing.

Presentation issues are frequent enough to affect technical clarity, including grammar errors, inconsistent terminology, duplicated/odd references, and mismatched claims versus tables. These are partly fixable, but in several places they obscure what was actually evaluated.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of common VFI pipelines: independently interpolating short frame triplets can produce long-range temporal inconsistency, especially at high interpolation factors.

The proposed formulation of chunk-level autoregressive latent generation with diffusion forcing is a plausible direction for video-centric VFI, and the skip-concatenate sampling idea is simple and potentially useful for reducing drift.

The paper includes ablations for the main proposed components. Table 2 suggests skip-concatenate sampling improves FVD substantially over causal autoregressive sampling, and the conditional VAE improves LPIPS.

The method is practically ambitious: it attempts long-sequence interpolation, high interpolation factors up to 16x, and high-resolution inference through tiling, sparse attention, and sequence parallelism.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main comparison includes only RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, and BiM-VFI, while omitting several directly relevant diffusion-based VFI methods discussed in the paper, such as LDMVFI, EDEN, LBBDM, MADIFF, and VIDIM. This makes the claimed state-of-the-art status weakly supported.

The quantitative results do not consistently show superiority. In Table 1, LDF-VFI is not best on LPIPS for SNU-FILM-4x, SNU-FILM-16x, or XTest-16x, and the gains are mainly in FVD. The text nevertheless claims broadly superior performance, and even refers to SNU-FILM-hard/extreme and XTest-4K splits that are not what Table 1 reports, creating confusion about what was actually evaluated.

The benchmark protocol is problematic and under-specified. The authors introduce new 'entire' benchmarks derived from existing datasets, but do not provide enough detail about splits, number of videos, sequence lengths, downsampling details, or FVD computation. Since the core evidence relies on these new benchmarks, this significantly hurts reproducibility and comparability.

Several major technical claims are overstated or unsupported. The paper claims arbitrary-resolution or 4K generalization and says computation is decoupled from image resolution, but local attention and tiled VAE still scale with the number of tiles/pixels. The only practical statement is that two 80GB GPUs suffice for 4K inference, which is not evidence of resolution-independent cost or broad arbitrary-resolution generalization.

The skip-concatenate method is not convincingly validated for long-range error accumulation. The paper claims constant-level error over arbitrary video duration, but the ablation only reports aggregate LPIPS/FVD on short benchmark videos and does not show error-vs-time curves, boundary continuity analysis, or comparisons over genuinely long sequences.

The method description lacks important implementation details needed for reproduction, including model size, exact sparse attention windowing, chunk scheduling for skip-concatenate sampling, inference chunk overlap/boundary handling, FVD protocol, and benchmark construction. The abstract says source code is available but the URL is blank.

The paper depends heavily on large pretrained components and large-scale training, including Wan2.1 initialization and LAVIB, but the contribution of the proposed modeling choices versus pretrained video prior/data scale is not disentangled. There is no comparison to a similarly initialized non-autoregressive or full-context baseline.

The ablations are incomplete. There is no ablation of sparse attention versus full/local alternatives, temporal chunk length, tiled VAE effects on quality/boundaries, number of sampling steps, or the cost-quality tradeoff. The conditional VAE ablation also changes reconstruction capacity, so it is hard to isolate whether improvements come from the proposed conditioning mechanism specifically.

The presentation contains many grammatical and formatting issues, awkward phrasing, inconsistent naming, and table/text mismatches. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they make an already under-specified method harder to assess.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of standard VFI pipelines: treating interpolation as independent adjacent-frame triplets can produce temporally inconsistent long sequences. The proposed video-centric formulation is well motivated and useful for high-rate and long-form interpolation.

The technical design is coherent: latent flow/diffusion modeling, chunk-level diffusion forcing, local spatial/full temporal attention, tiled VAE encoding, and a conditional VAE decoder all target concrete bottlenecks in long, high-resolution VFI.

The skip-concatenate sampling idea is a meaningful contribution for this setting. The ablation shows a clear FVD improvement over causal AR sampling with the same unconditioned decoder, e.g. average FVD drops from 22.67 to 17.05, supporting the claim that it improves temporal stability.

The empirical results are strong on the proposed video-centric benchmarks. LDF-VFI obtains the best FVD across SNU-FILM 4x/8x/16x and XTest 16x, with especially large gains at higher interpolation factors, where temporal coherence matters most.

The paper includes relevant component ablations for AR order, conditional VAE, and nearest-neighbor temporal upsampling. These make the performance gains more attributable than a single end-to-end comparison would.
The qualitative examples are consistent with the quantitative story: the proposed method visibly reduces severe artifacts in challenging large-motion cases such as bird-wing and skateboard motion.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrower than the strength of the claims. The main comparisons are on newly constructed video-centric variants of SNU-FILM and XTest, while conventional VFI benchmarks and recently competitive diffusion-based VFI methods such as LDMVFI, EDEN, LBBDM, MADIFF, and VIDIM are not quantitatively compared. This limits confidence that the method is broadly state of the art rather than strong under the proposed protocol.

Some claims are overstated or insufficiently substantiated. The manuscript claims arbitrary-resolution or 4K generalization without retraining, but the evidence appears limited to XTest-16x/4K-style evaluation and reports that 4K inference needs two 80GB GPUs. There is no runtime, memory, scaling, or resolution-ablation table to support the efficiency and scalability claims quantitatively.

The new benchmark protocol is not described in enough detail for full reproducibility. The paper states that low-frame-rate inputs are constructed by downsampling entire test videos, but details such as exact clip selection, number of videos for XTest, temporal lengths, preprocessing, FVD computation settings, and whether all methods receive comparable temporal information are under-specified.

The comparison may favor the proposed paradigm because frame-pair baselines are run frame-by-frame even though the benchmarks allow access to the whole low-frame-rate video. This is reasonable for models that cannot use longer context, but it makes the headline comparison partly a protocol mismatch; stronger long-context or diffusion baselines would make the evidence more convincing.

The ablations do not isolate several important design choices. There is no ablation of local sparse attention versus fuller attention at feasible resolution, tiled versus non-tiled VAE behavior, temporal chunk length, skip interval, number of sampling steps, or conditioning strategy beyond nearest-neighbor versus zero padding for VAE reconstruction.

Reproducibility has notable gaps. The abstract says source code is available but no URL is provided. The architecture description lacks some implementation specifics needed to reproduce the sparse attention pattern, chunk scheduling, skip-concatenate order, and conditional VAE integration exactly.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: there are typos and grammatical errors, Table 1 is described using split names that do not match the table text, and parts of the method use imprecise wording such as the skip-concatenate strategy achieving error accumulation at a constant level without a formal or empirical long-horizon validation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of frame-centric VFI: independently interpolating triplets can produce temporal inconsistency. The proposed video-centric formulation, chunk-level latent generation, and autoregressive inference are well motivated for high interpolation factors and longer clips.

The method combines several practical components into a coherent system: diffusion/flow matching in latent space, local spatial but dense temporal attention, tiled VAE encoding, nearest-neighbor conditioning with a mask, skip-concatenate sampling, and a conditional VAE decoder.

The empirical results are promising, especially on temporal metrics. LDF-VFI achieves the best FVD across the reported SNU-FILM-entire and X4K-entire settings, with notable gains at 16x interpolation and on 4K videos.

The ablations are useful: skip-concatenate sampling improves average FVD over causal AR sampling, the conditional VAE improves LPIPS, sparse attention substantially improves 4K efficiency/generalization, and nearest-neighbor temporal upsampling improves key-frame reconstruction.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level. Much of the system builds on existing video latent diffusion/flow models, diffusion forcing, tiled VAE processing, ControlNet-style conditioning, and sparse attention. The main new idea, skip-concatenate sampling, is plausible but remains a heuristic with limited analysis.

The evaluation is strongly centered on newly constructed 'entire' benchmarks and FVD-like temporal metrics. Standard VFI benchmarks and pixel-fidelity metrics are largely omitted, making it hard to compare with the broader literature and to understand tradeoffs where generative interpolation may hallucinate plausible but inaccurate content.

The claimed state-of-the-art performance is not uniform. LDF-VFI is not best on several per-frame or motion-aware metrics: for example EDEN has better LPIPS on SNU-FILM-4x/8x, BiM-VFI has better LPIPS and FloLPIPS on X4K-16x, and VFIPS is sometimes worse than baselines. The paper should phrase claims more carefully around temporal consistency/FVD rather than general SOTA.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. Many compared methods are frame-centric and are run recursively/frame-by-frame, while the proposed method is explicitly designed for full-video context and trained on large-scale LAVIB with WAN2.1 initialization. The paper does not deeply control for training data, model scale, or access to context.

The evidence for arbitrary-length temporal stability is limited. The benchmarks appear to use relatively short clips, and the paper does not report long-video stress tests, error growth over many chunks, or failure cases where skip chunks generated without immediate context may create discontinuities.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says source code is available but the URL is blank, and important implementation details such as model size, exact sparse-attention windowing, dataset construction/splits, training cost, and inference memory are not sufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

strengths: The paper tackles an important limitation of many VFI systems: frame-triplet inference can produce temporal inconsistency when many intermediate frames are generated. The proposed video-centric formulation is a reasonable direction for long-range coherence.

The architecture combines several plausible components for high-resolution long-video interpolation: latent-space generation, spatially local/temporally dense attention, tiled VAE encoding, autoregressive temporal chunks, and a conditional VAE decoder.

The empirical results show meaningful gains on the authors' video-centric benchmarks in FVD, especially for high interpolation factors. The ablation in Table 3 supports that skip-concatenate sampling improves FVD over causal AR sampling, and the conditional VAE improves LPIPS.
The paper includes useful efficiency and design ablations, including sparse versus full attention and sampling-step tradeoffs, which help explain some engineering choices.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The method is claimed to achieve state-of-the-art performance, but it is not best on many reported per-frame/perceptual metrics: for example EDEN is better on SNU-FILM-4x LPIPS and FloLPIPS, BiM-VFI is better on X4K LPIPS/VFIPS/FloLPIPS, and the proposed method's strongest advantage is mainly FVD.

The evaluation relies on newly constructed 'entire' benchmarks, while standard VFI benchmarks are not reported. This makes it difficult to compare with the broader literature and to assess whether the method improves VFI generally rather than under a benchmark design favoring long-context models.

The comparison to prior methods is not fully satisfying. Baselines that only operate on adjacent frames are run frame-by-frame, but the paper does not compare against stronger adaptations that could use longer temporal context, nor does it isolate whether gains come from the video-centric paradigm, large pretrained Wan2.1 initialization, the new decoder, or benchmark construction.

The method is computationally heavy. On SNU-FILM-8x, LDF-VFI at 16 steps is 3.36 s/frame versus 0.15 s/frame for BiM-VFI, and on X4K it requires multi-GPU USP with 16.3 s/frame. This substantially weakens the practical usefulness claim, especially for VFI applications where speed matters.

The arbitrary-length and error-accumulation claims are not adequately validated. The paper shows a qualitative/limited temporal-discontinuity analysis and FVD on short benchmarks, but does not provide long-duration stress tests, drift curves over many chunks, or failure cases for skip-concatenate sampling.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says source code is available but the URL is blank; important implementation details such as model size, attention window sizes, training data preprocessing, benchmark splits, exact evaluation protocol, and baseline inference settings are insufficiently specified.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. Many ingredients are borrowed or adapted from existing video diffusion/flow-matching, diffusion forcing, ControlNet-like conditioning, Wan VAE/DiT, tiled encoding, and sparse attention. The paper's main contribution is an engineering combination plus a sampling order, but the conceptual advance is not deeply analyzed.

The manuscript has clarity and polish issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology, crowded tables, and some ambiguous descriptions of skip-concatenate scheduling and temporal chunk construction. These are not the core reason for rejection, but they make the technical claims harder to verify.

strengths: The paper proposes a timely and useful reframing of VFI from independent triplet prediction to video-level generation. The central design, LDF-VFI, combines autoregressive chunked latent diffusion/flow matching with temporally dense but spatially local attention, which is well aligned with the stated goals of long-video coherence and high-resolution scalability.

The empirical gains are meaningful on the proposed video-centric benchmarks. LDF-VFI obtains the best FVD across SNU-FILM-entire 4x/8x/16x and X4K-entire 16x, with especially large improvements at high interpolation factors, supporting the claim that video-level modeling improves temporal consistency.

The ablations are relevant and mostly convincing. Skip-concatenate sampling improves average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05 over causal AR, the conditional VAE improves LPIPS substantially, sparse attention is much faster and better than full attention at high resolution, and nearest-neighbor temporal conditioning is justified by reconstruction results.

The method addresses practical scaling issues often ignored in diffusion-based VFI: tiled VAE encoding, sparse attention, temporal chunking, and USP inference are described together as a coherent system capable of 4K inference.
Qualitative examples and temporal-slice analysis support the quantitative story, particularly for large motion where frame-centric methods blur or distort intermediate frames.
weaknesses: The evaluation is centered on newly constructed 'entire video' variants of SNU-FILM and X4K, but the manuscript does not provide enough detail about benchmark sizes, splits, or statistical reliability. This makes it harder to judge whether the FVD gains are robust, especially since FVD can be unstable for small video sets.

Comparisons may not be fully balanced. Most baselines are pairwise VFI methods run frame-by-frame, while the proposed method is designed to exploit full low-frame-rate videos. This is a valid use case, but the paper should more carefully separate gains from the new task formulation versus gains from architecture/training scale.

The method is computationally heavy. At 16 steps it requires 3.36 s/frame on SNU-FILM-8x and 16.3 s/frame on X4K-16x using 4 GPUs, substantially slower than strong flow-based baselines. The 2-step variant is more practical but loses some quality; the tradeoff weakens claims of broad real-world applicability.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence shown. The paper claims arbitrary-length stability and arbitrary-resolution generalization, but experiments mainly cover fixed benchmark settings and 4K inference. There is no systematic stress test over video duration, resolution, or chunk-boundary frequency.

The novelty is partly architectural integration rather than a single clearly isolated algorithmic advance. Diffusion forcing, autoregressive video diffusion, tiled VAE processing, local attention, and ControlNet-like conditional decoding are all existing ideas; skip-concatenate sampling is the most distinctive piece, but its comparison set is limited mainly to causal AR/non-AR variants.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The abstract says source code is available, but no URL is visible in the provided text, and several implementation details needed to reproduce the full system, such as exact benchmark construction protocol, sparse attention window configuration, and inference chunk scheduling, are underspecified.
